L312: P - BIOL-L 211 or BIOL-S 211
This course is designed to understand how and why cell
biology is key to understanding and unlocking many aspects
of human biology and evolution of life in all its forms.
There is an emphasis on eukaryotic organisms. We will focus
on the structure, function and biosynthesis of cellular
membranes and organelles; protein transport and modification
in the cell; the cytoskeleton; cell signaling, cell growth,
cell death* and how they are impacted in disease states via
Bench to Bedside lectures.   The focus of the course is to
learn cell biology while engaging in core scientific
practices essential for a biology major and for success in
your future professional goals.   For those, whose future
goals involves healthcare the "premed competencies" as
defined by American Association of Medical Colleges we will
engage in are  Scientific Inquiry. Applies knowledge of the
scientific process to integrate and synthesize information,
solve problems, and formulate research questions and
hypotheses; is facile in the language of the sciences and
uses it to participate in the discourse of science and
explain how scientific knowledge is discovered and
validated? and Written Communication. Effectively conveys
information to others by using written words and sentences.
Note: To achieve the objectives above this class uses a
"flipped format" where class time will be used through
active learning, learning how to deconstruct a paper using a
method called C.R.E.A.T.E (see here:
https://iu.mediaspace.kaltura.com/media/t/1_iyonp779) , and
exploring the connection between Cell Biology and medicine
through Bench to Bedside activities.  Students will not be
getting a traditional lecture in class! You will be expected
to complete assigned readings/videos before class.

Topic: The Science of Choice: Foundations. From the trivial
(which shirt should I buy?) to the significant (where should
I go to college?), our choices play an enormous role in
making us who we are. To improve our decisions, we must
first better understand the psychological processes that
unfold when making choices. The purpose of this course is to
introduce you to the fundamentals of the scientific study of
human judgment and decision making. We will cover topics
like when to trust expert advice, when to "go with your
gut", how moral judgments are made, and maybe even choosing
a romantic partner. Most importantly, by learning the
techniques decision scientists use to study these topics you
can begin to develop empirically supported strategies for
your own decisions.

Topic: Neuroepigenetics and Clinical Disorders. Our
behaviors emerge from the brain's intricate networks. This
course examines how epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA
methylation and histone modifications shape neural function
and behavior. We will explore how these processes contribute
to the development and progression of clinical conditions,
including mental illness, neurodegenerative diseases, and
addiction. Broader discussions will also consider how
environmental and experiential factors can influence the
epigenome across the lifespan.

Topic:  Neurobiology of Cognition. The course aims to
provide deep insights into the neurobiology of cognition
from a top-down perspective. Specifically, the neuronal
mechanisms underlying cognitive processes are introduced in
the light of the newest research. To further the
understanding of cognition, we cover the organization
principles of cortical networks both at the structural and
functional levels. In addition, the diversity of cell types
and their networks in the cerebral cortex are introduced
together with the communication features between nerve cells
within the cortical areas and between cortical and
subcortical regions. In addition, the course provides
fundamental knowledge of the basis of the cellular and
circuit mechanisms underlying the generation of brain
rhythms such as theta and gamma oscillations linked to
cognitive functions. Furthermore, some of the key cortical
structures, including the hippocampus, amygdala and
prefrontal cortex are reviewed in detail as these regions
play a critical role in many higher order cognitive
functions, such as place coding, emotional memory formation,
decision-making, empathy.

Topic: The Neuroscience of Mood Disorders. This course
provides an in-depth exploration of the neurobiological
mechanisms underlying mood disorders. Mood disorders are
mental health conditions that primarily affects an
individuals emotional state. We will explore depression and
its subtypes, bipolar disorder and its subtypes,
premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and disruptive mood
dysregulation disorder. We will investigate mood disorders
through multiple neuroscience lenses including clinical,
preclinical, systems, cellular and molecular neuroscience,
as well as from an environmental and cultural perspective.
This course is set up as half lecture and half seminar
involving class discussion, student interaction, and debate.
We will utilize current and classic findings from human and
non-human animal studies to drive our discussions.

Topic: The Neuroscience of Psychedelics. We are in the midst
of a "psychedelic renaissance", with a renewed and explosive
growth in interest into how psychedelic drugs alter
consciousness, brain function and brain connectivity, and
produce enduring improvements in mental health. This course
will address the neurobiological mechanisms of action of
various classic and atypical psychedelic drugs, the
resulting changes in brain activity, their therapeutic
potential, the possible risks associated with their use, and
integration of the neurobiological perspective with
traditional religious, mystical, and anthropological
viewpoints.

Topic: The Psychology of Attractiveness and Dating. What
determines who we are attracted to? What evolutionary,
societal, and biological pressures influence physical
attractiveness? How does attractiveness influence mate
selection through the dating process? How many people should
you date before choosing a life partner? In this course we
will address the psychological literature that summarizes
and models dating interactions. We will focus on data
collection that addresses the dimensions of attractiveness,
as well as the barriers to successful dating.

Topic: The Psychology of Death. This course provides an
introduction to the study of death and dying, spanning
biological, developmental, social, and clinical perspectives
on death. The goals of the course are to (1) provide
foundational knowledge on the psychology of death through
readings, mini-lectures, and in-class discussions, and (2)
aid the development of higher-order thinking skills,
including understanding complex texts, integrating
interdisciplinary perspectives, and building and evaluating
arguments.

Topic: Neurobiology of Neurodegenerative Diseases. The goal
of this Topics course will be to investigate what is
currently known about the main neurodegenerative diseases
(including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's,
frontotemporal dementia) and investigate current drug
therapies. In this pursuit, we will be discussing cutting
edge developments in the field and exploring the challenges
that underlie the many failed therapeutic approaches. More
specifically: we will get elbows-deep in the literature for
these various neurodegenerative disorders and critically
evaluate the findings and implications. Learning will
include a combination of lecture, student presentations, and
class discussions.

Topic: Diagnosing and Treating Eating Disorders. We begin
the semester by reviewing the diagnostic criteria and
evidence-based assessment tools for anorexia nervosa,
bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and avoidant and
restrictive food intake disorder, including their
overlapping traits and characteristics. Next, we delve
deeply dive three empirically-supported treatments for
eating disorders: Enhanced Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for
the Transdiagnostic Treatment of Eating Disorders, Family
Based Therapy for Childhood Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia
Nervosa, and The Body Project, an eating disorder prevention
program. Finally, students will explore topics related to
eating disorders that they are most interested in (e.g.,
food addiction, clinical presentations of eating disorders
cross culturally), in the form of group project and
presentations. This course operates like an upper-level
seminar and emphasizes small and large group discussions,
projects, and in-class skill practice. Most of our time is
spent doing clinical skills rather than discussing them
theoretically. Please note that we will approach the
diagnosis and treatment of eating disorders from an
empirical lens. If you have a personal history with an
eating disorder or are current struggling with disordered
eating and will find it difficult to engage with the course
material in a scientifically-rigorous manner, now may not be
the best time to take this class.

Topic: Clinical Psych & Neurosci in Developing Countries.
This course examines topics in clinical psychology and human
clinical neuroscience from a global mental health
perspective. To date, almost everything that we think we
know about clinical psychology and neuroscience comes from
studies conducted in populations that are Western, educated,
industrialized, rich, and democratic (so called "WEIRD"
populations from high-income countries). However, these
"WEIRD" populations represent a small percentage of the
worlds population (<15%); thus, raising critical questions
about whether current understanding of psychological and
neuroscience phenomena applies to the vast majority of the
worlds population living in middle- and low-income
countries. If you are interested in the foundations of
clinical psychology, such as assessment, treatment, and
prevention, and/or cross-cultural human clinical
neuroscience, then this course will be of particular
interest to you. We will address questions such as: what is
the current state of knowledge in global mental health
research and practice?; what is the magnitude of the global
mental health burden (i.e., amount of distress/disability)?;
do psychiatric categories and diagnoses differ across
cultures?; how can we test if assessment tools are
comparable across cultural contexts?; do social and
environmental determinants of mental health differ
cross-culturally?; how can we develop, adapt, and test
treatments in different global contexts?; and, in all of
these issues, what can mental health researchers and
practitioners in high-income countries learn from practices
developed in low and middle-income countries? The instructor
will draw heavily on clinical psychology and neuroscience
laboratory collaborations he has developed at Moi University
in Kenya, Africa.

Topic: Criminal Behavior. This course will address
biopsychosocial factors in criminal behavior from the
perspective of clinical psychology. The content will
emphasize personality constructs, psychopathology
(particularly psychopathy) and other fundamental
psychological factors in criminal behavior with reviews of
historical attempts to understand the psychological
complexity of criminal acts. Significant attention will be
devoted to the seemingly most inexplicable criminal
behaviors involving extreme violence such as often seen in
serial and mass murder. The course will include clinical
case studies and selected research studies to illuminate the
complex factors affecting etiology, treatment, and
prevention of criminal behavior.

Topic: Psychosis: Theory, Diagnoses, and Treatment.   This
course will explore the concept of psychosis, or "madness,"
as it is understood in psychology, psychiatry, and
philosophy. We will cover historical texts, first-person
accounts, and empirical research articles to build an
understanding of schizophrenia and related disorders. This
course will also cover sociocultural perspectives and
standards for diagnosis and treatment.

column5: Above class open to graduates only
Above class meets with REL-R 767, CULS-C 701, and CMLT-C 647
Topic: This seminar considers music as an expressive
dimension of religious conversion. Drawing on four case
studies (Gustav Mahlers conversion to Catholicism to
appease antisemitic leaders of the Vienna State Opera; John
Cages embracing of Zen Buddhism; Alice Coltrane's movement
from an Afro-Protestant-influenced jazz background to
Vedantic Hinduism; and Bob Dylans turn to evangelical
Christianity and Gospel music) well consider the politics
of conversion and its vagaries, religious and cultural
dimensions of sincerity and authenticity, questions of
appropriation, and religious and theological significations
of word and sound. Weekly assignments will include readings
in primary and secondary sources and listening to musical
examples. Students are encouraged to develop a term paper
that addresses issues from the course in their own areas of
interest or specialization

RSTR
This course is designed to analyze and investigate
sustainability reporting topics, including environmental,
social, and governance through multiple stakeholder lenses,
including present and potential investors, managers, the
media, consumers, and jurisdictions. We will explore
sustainability reporting as it relates to traditional
financial reporting, analyze regulatory requirements around
the world, and investigate stakeholder roles in
sustainability reporting. To accomplish these goals, we will
investigate current and proposed sustainability standards at
the general and industry-specific level and evaluate
multinational companies' sustainability reports.

column2: EDUC-F 203  TOP EXPLORATION IN EDUCATION (3 CR)

column3: VT: MEDIA MESSAGES: POWER AND IDEN

column5: What can we learn from TikTok, advertisements, and movies?
More broadly, how does the media depict race, gender, class,
and sexuality as well as the intersection of these
identities? In this course, you will learn how to creatively
analyze and critique messages of power, knowledge, and
social structures in media. You will also use innovative
methods, such as poetry, photography, and collage to explore
your identities and challenge taken-for-granted messages
about race, gender, class, and sexuality

Above class is a Service Learning Course
Description: In this service-learning course, students will
engage in workshops/learning activities for academic and
professional support. A major emphasis in the course will be
exploring and preparing applications for various STEM
opportunities - research experiences for undergraduates,
internships, and more. Over the course of the semester,
students will also engage in service at the WonderLab Museum
of Science, Health, and Technology. The overall goal of the
course is to support students to develop key academic and
professional skills necessary for success in college, with a
focus on STEM.
This course will explore the characteristics of today's
college student. As a class we will interrogate the
following question: Who are today's college students? In
order to unpack this question further we will examine how
the identities, demographics, and experiences of college
students changed over time to create the "contemporary"
college student. Additionally, we will seek to understand
current trends in higher education and their implications on
today's college student. Does not require permission.

Are you dreading an upcoming test? Do you blank out or have
trouble focusing every time you take a big exam? Are you
frustrated because you consistently find that your scores do
not match what you feel you really know? Preparing for an
important professional school entrance exam like the MCAT,
LSAT, etc.? This course is all about evidence-backed
strategies for taking your anxiety level way down for any
kind of test, whether that be for professional school
entrance exams or finals in your most difficult courses. Our
approach centers on how to 1) apply the science of powerful
learning to better prepare for important tests; 2) create
effective schedules and habits for studying so it sticks;
and 3) transform the emotions that come up before, during,
and after the test to achieve your performance and
professional goals.

education and will create a resource bank of instructional
materials to use in future classrooms.

column5: Misguided Medicine is going to be an online synchronous
course. In this course, you will listen to episodes of the
podcast Sawbones, and dive into the misguided nature/history
of some anatomy/physiology based studies. Each week, well
explore a different body system by listening to episodes
that uncover the strange, misguided, and fascinating history
of medicine. Then we will dive into meaningful ethical
discussions and clinical considerations related to those
systems. Assessments and guided conversations will help
connect past mistakes to modern healthcare practice. Credits
count towards the Minor in Medical Sciences!
